name: musical-terms

description.en: 61 Italian terms from sheet music for tempo, dynamics, articulation and expression, from adagio and allegro to crescendo, staccato and dolce. The Italian term on the front, with its usual abbreviation where it has one; what it asks of the performer on the back, in English and Swedish, in our own words. Tempo terms describe a character, not a metronome figure. Checked against Theodore Baker's Dictionary of Musical Terms (1904), in the public domain, and Karl Gehrkens' Music Notation and Terminology (1914), in the public domain in the United States, with Wiktionary and Svensk ordbok.
description.sv: 61 italienska termer ur notblad för tempo, dynamik, artikulation och uttryck, från adagio och allegro till crescendo, staccato och dolce. Den italienska termen på framsidan, med sin vanliga förkortning om den har någon; vad den ber musikern om på baksidan, på engelska och svenska, med egna ord. Tempotermerna beskriver en karaktär, inte en metronomsiffra. Kontrollerade mot Theodore Bakers Dictionary of Musical Terms (1904), fri från upphovsrätt, och Karl Gehrkens Music Notation and Terminology (1914), fri från upphovsrätt i USA, samt Wiktionary och Svensk ordbok.

method: Choosing the content sources. Card content may only come from openly licensed or public-domain sources, so the meanings come from two public-domain reference works: Theodore Baker's A Dictionary of Musical Terms (G. Schirmer, 1904 printing of the 1895 work), whose OCR text was downloaded from the Internet Archive (item cu31924017810106, file cu31924017810106_djvu.txt, found with the archive.org advanced search API), and Karl W. Gehrkens' Music Notation and Terminology (1914), downloaded as plain text from Project Gutenberg (eBook #19499). Both were saved unchanged in the scratch directory. The exact commands are under Queries.

Choosing the terms. The deck editor's brief asked for about 60 Italian terms for tempo, dynamics, articulation and expression. A candidate list of 67 terms was drawn up from the terms both books treat as basic: Gehrkens' tempo groups (chapter XI, §109), his tempo changes (§§111–113), his dynamics list (chapter XIII, §§120–127), his signs and repeats (chapters IV–V) and his expression terms (§130), cross-checked with Baker's article Tempo-mark and his table of abbreviations. Six candidates were then left out for the reasons under Selection (andantino, ritenuto, fermata, stringendo, l'istesso tempo, con sordino), leaving 61. The selection is the standard core vocabulary of any music-theory course; it was not copied from a list in any one source.

Finding each term in the sources. For each term the Gehrkens text was searched for the paragraph that defines it (e.g. sed -n 2150,2870p for the tempo and dynamics chapters) and Baker's OCR text for its entry with a small script (baker_grep.py) that ignores the stress marks Baker prints inside headwords (Alle'gro). Baker's two-column OCR is noisy; where an entry was garbled (Allegretto, Mezzo piano, Brio) the card relies on the other sources and Baker's quoted text in the evidence is only what is legible. In the quotations from Baker below, his stress marks are left out, and obvious OCR misreadings of single letters in the quoted words are corrected (for example 'pid mosso' to 'più mosso', 'Zegatis'simo' to 'legatissimo', 's/acc.' to 'stacc.'); where a passage was too garbled to correct, it is not quoted.

Writing the cards. The front is the Italian term as both books spell it, with accents as in modern Italian (più, not piu). A frontNote gives the abbreviation where Baker's table of abbreviations or Gehrkens gives one that is in common use (cresc., dim., rit., pp, sfz, D.C., pizz., espr., Tempo I). The back is a short definition in our own words in English, and the same in Swedish, giving the character of tempo terms rather than a metronome figure, since both books stress that tempo words are relative (Gehrkens §108–109: "no absolute rate of speed can be indicated"; Baker, Tempo-mark: "They do not in themselves indicate a fixed and positive rate of speed, but only the general character of the movement"). A backNote adds the literal meaning or a short disambiguation where it helps (allegro 'cheerful', rubato 'robbed', decrescendo = diminuendo).

Cross-checking each card. Every card was checked against both public-domain books where both cover the term. Each card was also checked against the English Wiktionary entry where one exists, fetched with the Wiktionary REST API (https://en.wiktionary.org/api/rest_v1/page/definition/<term>), whose English and Italian sections were read for the musical sense; Wiktionary has no entry for tempo primo, meno mosso and più mosso, so those three rest on the two books alone (36 cards quote Wiktionary in their evidence). The Swedish wording was written by the authoring agent as idiomatic Swedish, translating the meaning given by the content sources. It was checked against Svensk ordbok (Svenska Akademien), queried through the search API behind svenska.se (https://svenska.se/api/search/so?q=<term>), for the 30 cards whose term has its own SO entry in the musical sense (mezzoforte was found in review round 1 under its one-word spelling; SO's dacapo is only the encore sense). In review round 1, 12 cards were checked against the Swedish Wiktionary (11 not covered by SO, plus mezzo forte, which has both) (and the three mezzo/fortepiano dynamics also against Swedish Wikipedia's article Dynamik (musik)). For the remaining 20 cards (larghetto, prestissimo, allargando, a tempo, tempo primo, meno mosso, più mosso, morendo, marcato, tenuto, arco, dal segno, attacca, grazioso, leggiero, tranquillo, sotto voce, pesante, giocoso, poco a poco) no Swedish reference with the term was found: their Swedish back is the authoring agent's translation of the English definition, not checked against a Swedish reference. Each card's evidence quotes what each source actually says, as seen on 2026-10-04.

Machine checks against Wikidata. One SPARQL query (under Queries) looked up every Wikidata item whose Italian label is one of the candidate terms, with its English and Swedish labels, descriptions and P31 classes; a few items were then read with wbgetentities. Where an item is clearly the musical term (by its description, its P31 'musical concept' Q115211517, 'dynamics' Q113558 or 'articulation' Q372923, or its sitelinks), the card has a check that the item's Italian label equals the front. 39 cards have such a check; the builder (authored_decks.py check/build) runs them against live Wikidata. Many common terms (piano, forte, dolce, fine, arco, grave, corona) have no musical item with that Italian label, only homonyms (plan, fort, sweetness, end, bow, falling body, crown), so those cards have no check. Wikidata descriptions were not used for content: several disagree with the reference works (see Quality control).

Who did the work. The research, the drafting and the cross-checking were done by AI agents (Claude, Anthropic) at Anton Wiklund's direction, with machine checks (the builder's dossier validation and Wikidata checks, and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and three independent AI review rounds (factual accuracy; language and translation; licensing, attribution and documentation), logged as rounds 1–3 under Quality control. The cards have not yet been reviewed by a human subject expert.
selection: Included: 61 Italian (or, for glissando, Italian-formed) performance directions that appear on the music itself and are part of the basic vocabulary every music-theory primer teaches: 12 tempo marks from grave to prestissimo, 9 changes of tempo (accelerando, ritardando, rallentando, allargando, a tempo, tempo primo, rubato, meno mosso, più mosso), 12 dynamic marks and changes (pianissimo to fortissimo, crescendo, decrescendo, diminuendo, sforzando, fortepiano, morendo), 8 terms for articulation and playing technique (staccato, legato, marcato, tenuto, pizzicato, arco, glissando, tutti), 4 road-map terms (da capo, dal segno, fine, attacca), 12 expression terms (dolce, cantabile, espressivo, grazioso, maestoso, agitato, con brio, leggiero, tranquillo, sotto voce, pesante, giocoso) and 4 modifiers that combine with all the others (molto, poco a poco, sempre, subito). Left out: andantino, because the sources disagree on whether it is faster or slower than andante (Gehrkens §109 notes it is 'now quite universally taken slightly faster than andante' although the word means 'less going'), so the card would have no single right answer; ritenuto, because whether it differs from ritardando (immediately slower rather than gradually) is contested (Gehrkens §111 says most composers do not distinguish them, Baker says it is 'often used incorrectly for rallentando'); fermata, because the card would not have one clean answer: Baker lists both Corona (It.) 'A hold' and Fermata (It.) with 'A hold' only as its second sense after 'a pause, stop, or interruption'; Gehrkens uses fermata as the English name of the sign; Wikidata Q830328 (the sign) has the Italian label 'corona'; and the Italian word fermata also means a stop; stringendo, l'istesso tempo and con sordino, to keep the deck near the brief's 60 cards with the most common terms. Also left out: names of forms and pieces (sonata, scherzo, toccata), voice types, instrument names, French and German terms, Latin terms (ad libitum) and metronome ranges, which vary between sources.

licensing: The deck is CC0 1.0. Its two content sources are in the public domain: Baker's dictionary was published in 1895/1904 and its author died in 1934, so it is free both in the United States and under life + 70 years terms; Gehrkens' book was published in the United States in 1914 and is in the public domain there. Because Gehrkens died in 1975 his text may still be protected elsewhere, so from both books the deck takes only facts (what a term means, how it is abbreviated), which are not protected by copyright, and states them in its own words; no definition is copied, though a few short standard glosses (such as 'in a singing style', 'held for its full value') coincide with the books' wording. The selection of terms is the standard core vocabulary of performance directions, assembled for this deck from the topics both books cover, not copied from any list. Wikidata (CC0) was used only for machine checks of the Italian spelling. Wiktionary in English and Swedish (CC BY-SA 4.0; the English edition dual-licensed with the GFDL), Swedish Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Svensk ordbok (© Svenska Akademien) were consulted only to confirm meanings and Swedish usage: no selection was taken from any of them, and no wording beyond single ordinary words and common short phrases that any translation of the content sources would use (for example 'medelstarkt' for Gehrkens' 'medium loudly'). In review round 3 the backs whose wording followed Wiktionary more closely than the content sources (glissando, con brio, mezzo piano) were rewritten from Baker and Gehrkens. Their share-alike conditions and reserved rights therefore do not apply to the deck.

rounds.lens: Source agreement, licence policy and Wikidata machine checks
rounds.scope: All 61 cards and the six candidates that were left out
rounds.summary: Every card's meaning was confirmed in at least two sources, at least one of them a public-domain content source (Baker and/or Gehrkens), and in most cases also in Wiktionary or Svensk ordbok. The builder's Wikidata checks cover the Italian spelling of 39 fronts (the Italian label of the item for the musical term); they all pass. Wikidata's descriptions were compared with the reference works and not used, because several disagree with them. Terms on which the sources disagree were left out or given the convention in a note.

findings.issue: Gehrkens §109: andantino 'is now quite universally taken slightly faster than andante' although by its form it means 'going less', i.e. more slowly; Baker's article Tempo-mark places it among the slow terms. The front would not have one right answer.
findings.resolution: Left out of the deck.

findings.issue: Baker: 'Properly, held back, in slower tempo; but often used incorrectly for rallentando'. Gehrkens §111: some composers distinguish ritenuto (definitely slower) from ritardando (gradually slower), 'the majority of composers do not'. Contested.
findings.resolution: Left out of the deck; ritardando and rallentando, on which the sources agree, are in.

findings.issue: The pause sign is called corona in Italian: Wikidata Q830328 (the musical symbol) has the Italian label 'corona' and no 'fermata'; the only Italian 'fermata' items are a bus stop (Q548662) and a legal term (Q106451578). Gehrkens and Baker use 'fermata' as the English name. A card with 'fermata' tagged as Italian would be wrong. [Corrected in round 3: Baker labels Fermata as Italian ("Fermata (It.) … 2. A hold") and also lists "Corona (It.) A hold"; only Gehrkens uses fermata as the English name. The exclusion stands: two Italian names and an ambiguous Italian word give no single clean answer.]
findings.resolution: Left out of the deck.

findings.issue: Gehrkens, footnote 28, records an old dispute over whether allegretto is faster or slower than allegro, but concludes it is 'usually interpreted as meaning a tempo somewhat slower than allegro'; Wiktionary's allegro entry ('faster than allegretto') and SO ('i relativt livligt tempo') agree with the usual reading.
findings.resolution: Kept with the usual meaning (moderately fast, a little slower than allegro).

findings.issue: Is rallentando the same as ritardando? Gehrkens §111 lists both as gradual retards and says most composers do not distinguish them; Baker's abbreviation table and SO give both the same meaning ('så småningom långsammare').
findings.resolution: Both cards give the same meaning in different words; a backNote on rallentando says the two are used interchangeably. [Round 2: the note now reads 'Means the same as ritardando.']

findings.issue: Placement varies: Gehrkens puts vivace between allegro and presto, Baker says it calls for 'a movement equalling or exceeding allegro', Wikidata Q2096748 (presto) describes presto as 'lighter than vivace'.
findings.resolution: The back gives the character (lively, brisk) and says only 'usually faster than allegro', on which Gehrkens and Baker agree; the Wikidata description was not used. [Round 1: reworded to 'at least as fast as allegro', which matches both books exactly.]

findings.issue: Relative order of the slow tempos varies between sources: Wikidata Q482153 says adagio is 'between largo and andante', SO says largo and lento are 'något långsammare än adagio', Baker's Tempo-mark article groups grave, largo, lento and adagio together as 'slow'.
findings.resolution: The slow tempo cards give the character of each term (heavy and solemn, broad, at ease, simply slow) and do not rank them, except larghetto, which all sources describe as a little less slow than largo.

findings.issue: Gehrkens §112 treats 'a tempo' and 'tempo primo' alike as a return to the normal rate after a change; Baker gives 'tempo primo, return to the original tempo'; Wiktionary's Italian 'a tempo': 'return to normal tempo from a deviation'.
findings.resolution: a tempo: back to the normal tempo after a change; tempo primo: back to the original tempo (its literal meaning 'first tempo' in a note). [Round 1: Baker also equates them ('tempo, or tempo primo, return to the original tempo'); both cards now say in a backNote that the other is used the same way.]

findings.issue: Wiktionary gives leggiero as an alternative spelling of modern Italian leggero; scores and both reference books use leggiero.
findings.resolution: Front kept as leggiero, the spelling used in music; a backNote mentions leggero.

findings.issue: Wikidata Q2019172 has the Italian label 'più mosso' but English and Swedish labels without the accent ('piu mosso'); Gehrkens prints 'piu' without the accent (typographic limitation of the transcription).
findings.resolution: Front written with the accent, as in Italian and in Baker ('Più'); the check uses the Italian label.

findings.issue: Wikidata's item with the Italian label 'fortepiano' (Q1521313) is the early piano, not the dynamic; SO has both senses; Gehrkens writes the dynamic as 'forte piano'.
findings.resolution: No Wikidata check; front 'fortepiano' as in SO and Baker's table ('fp Forte piano'); a backNote mentions the instrument. [Round 3: the backNote now says 'an older name for the piano', which is what Baker ('Same as Pianoforte') and SO ('äldre benämning') say.]

findings.issue: Gehrkens defines glissando narrowly as a keyboard effect and says the word comes from French glisser; Baker gives bowed-string and piano senses; Wiktionary and SO give the general sense of sliding from one pitch to another.
findings.resolution: The back gives the general sense common to all of them; the French origin is in a backNote, citing Gehrkens. [Corrected in round 3: Gehrkens' keyboard-only sense is narrower; the general sense comes from Baker's sense 1(b), 'same as Portamento', i.e. 'a smooth gliding from one tone to another', confirmed by Wiktionary and SO. The back was reworded from Baker.]

findings.issue: Baker's OCR text of the entries Allegretto, Mezzo piano and Brio is garbled or cut off by the two-column layout.

evidence.says: Staccato (It.; superl. staccatissimo; abbr. stacc.) "Detached, separated"; noting a style in which the tones played or sung are more or less abruptly disconnected. The ordinary staccato is marked by round dots over or under the notes. Abbreviations table: "Stacc. Staccato"
A dot over or under a note is called the staccato mark and indicates that the tone is to be sounded and then instantly released. … Staccato—detached; the opposite of legato.
med tydligt uppehåll mellan tonerna vid sång el. instrumentspel; [underbetydelse, marked ‘äv. något utvidgat’:] hackigt eller stötvis (example ‘han talade stackato’)

back.en: Smoothly connected, with no gap between the notes

evidence.says: Legato (It.; superl. legatissimo.) "Bound"; a direction to perform the passage so marked in a smooth and connected manner, with no break between the tones
Legato—smoothly. … To indicate legato (sustained or connected) tones, as contrasted with staccato (detached) ones.
utan uppehåll mellan tonerna

evidence.locator: entry Marcato (OCR line 21982); table of abbreviations
evidence.says: Marcato (It., "marked".) … Marcatissimo, with very marked emphasis. Abbreviations table: "Marc. Marcato"
Ben—well. Ben marcato—well marked. … Sempre marcatissimo—always well marked, i.e., strongly accented.
stressed; pronounced. Italian: marked, accented

back.en: Each note held for its full value
back.sv: Varje ton hålls ut hela sitt notvärde

evidence.says: Tenuto (ten.) indicates that a tone or chord is to be held to its full value.
Tenuto (It., "held".) A direction signifying (a) generally, that a tone so marked is to be sustained for its full time-value
A tempo mark directing that a note or passage is to be held for the full time

back.en: Plucked with the fingers instead of bowed
back.sv: Knäppt med fingrarna i stället för spelat med stråke

evidence.says: Pizzicato—plucked. A term found in music for stringed instruments, and indicating that for the moment the bow is not to be used, the tone being secured by plucking the string.

evidence.locator: entry Pizzicato (OCR line 28366); table of abbreviations
evidence.says: Pizzicato (It., "pinched".) Plucked with the finger; a direction, in music for bow-instr.s, to play the notes so marked by plucking the strings. Abbreviations table: "Pizz. Pizzicato"
genom knäppning på strängarna (på stråkinstrumentet) med fingerspetsarna
Arco (It.) Bow; … coll'arco, with the bow, i. e. resume the bow after a Pizzicato passage
A note in string instrument musical notation indicating that the bow is to be used in the usual way, usually following a passage that is played pizzicato.

back.en: Gliding through the pitches between two notes
back.sv: Glidning genom tonhöjderna mellan två toner

backNote.en: An Italian-style word formed from French glisser, ‘to slide’.
backNote.sv: Ett italieniserat ord bildat av franskans glisser, ’glida’.

evidence.says: Glissando—playing a scale on the keyboard by drawing the finger along over the keys, thus depressing them in very rapid succession. The word is derived from the French word glisser—to glide.

Glissando (It.) 1. On bowed instr.s, (a) calls for a flowing, unaccented execution of a passage; (b) same as Portamento—2. On the pfte, a rapid scale-effect obtained by sliding the thumb, or thumb and one finger, over

Portamento (It.; equiv. to portar la voce, to carry the voice …) A smooth gliding from one tone to another; … It differs from the legato not only in its more deliberate execution, but also in the actual (though very rapid and slurring) sounding or passing-through the intermediate tones
Either a continuous sliding from one pitch to another ("true" glissando), or an incidental scale played while moving from one melodic note to another ("effective" glissando).
glidning från en ton till en annan längs skalan

back.en: All together: the whole ensemble performs

evidence.says: Tutti—(derived from totus, toti, Latin—all)—a direction signifying that all performers are to take part.
Tutti (pl.), in scores, indicates the entrance of the whole body of instrumentalists or vocalists after a solo
avsnitt i musikstycke där hela ensemblen eller stämman ska medverka
The words da capo (D.C.) mean literally "from the head," i.e., repeat from the beginning.
Capo (It.) The head, beginning… Da capo, from the beginning
From the beginning.
#(musik) från början, om igen, på nytt
The words dal segno (D.S.) indicate a repetition from the sign ([segno symbol] or [segno symbol]) instead of from the beginning.
Segno (It.) A sign… al segno, to the sign; Dal segno, from the sign,—directions to the performer to turn back and repeat from the place marked by the sign
From the last segno.

back.en: The end: the piece stops here after a repeat
back.sv: Slut: här slutar stycket efter en repris

evidence.says: In the case of both D.C. and D.S. the word fine (meaning literally the end) is ordinarily used to designate the point at which the repeated section is to terminate.
Fine (It.) End, close; indicates either the end of a repeated section (after the da capo or dal segno), or the end of a piece in several divisions.
The location in a musical score that indicates the end of the piece, particularly when the piece ends somewhere in the middle of the score due to a section of the music being repeated.
Italienska: #slut, ände

back.en: Go straight on to the next movement or section without a break
back.sv: Gå direkt vidare till nästa sats eller avsnitt utan uppehåll

evidence.says: Attacca—attack the next division without any pause.
Attacca (It.) Attack or begin what follows without pausing, or with a very short pause
Without any break between the current movement and the next movement of the work.
Dolce—sweetly, gently.

evidence.locator: entry Dolce (OCR line 11707); table of abbreviations
evidence.says: Dolce (It.) 1. Sweet, soft, suave; dolcemente, sweetly, softly. Abbreviations table: "Dol. Dolce"
på ett mjukt och milt sätt särsk. vid framförande av ett musikaliskt verk
Cantabile—in a singing style.
Cantabile (It.) In a singing or vocal style. Where a passage is so marked, the leading melody should stand out well from the accomp., and the general effect should be free and flowing.
Played in this style; singingly, lyrically
#(musik) sångbart
Espressivo—expressively.

evidence.locator: entry Espressione (OCR line 13081); table of abbreviations
evidence.says: Espressione, con (It.) With expression, expressively… Espressivo, expressive. Abbreviations table: "Espr., or Espress. Espressivo"
To be played in an expressive manner.
#(musik) uttrycksfullt
Grazioso—gracefully.

evidence.locator: article on Grazia and derived words (OCR lines 16767–16768)
evidence.says: Grazioso,-a, graceful, elegant… Graziosamente, gracefully.
gracefully, flowingly
Maesta, maestoso—majestically.
Maestoso (It.) Majestic, dignified
majestätiskt i fråga om utförande av musikstycke
Agitato—agitated.
Agitato, agitated; a. con passione, passionately agitated
Played in a restless agitated style.
#(musik) upprört, lidelsefullt
Brio (It.) Vivacity, spirit, fire
Allegro con brio—an allegro played in brilliant style. Faster than allegro.
With spirit, with vigor; vivaciously (used as a musical direction).
#(musik) livligt, eldigt

backNote.sv: På modern italienska stavas det leggero.

evidence.says: Leggiero—lightly.
Leggiero, a direction indicating, in piano-technic, that the passage is to be performed with as great lightness as is consistent with the degree of loudness required

evidence.locator: leggiero, English adverb and Italian adjective
evidence.says: Alternative form of leggero. Italian: alternative spelling of leggero
Tranquillo—tranquilly.
Tranquillamente (It.) Tranquilly, in a quiet style… Tranquillo, tranquil; often (with Beethoven) equiv. to moderato.
calm, sober, tranquil
Sotto—under. E.g., sotto voce—under the voice, i.e., with subdued tone. … Sotto voce—in subdued voice.
Sotto (It.) Below, under… Sottovoce, in an undertone, aside
Sung or played softly, instruments or voice.
Pesante (It.) Heavy, ponderous; calls for a firm and vigorous execution of the passages so marked.
Pesante—slowly, heavily.
heavy, ponderous
Giocoso,-a (It.) Playful, sportive, bantering; humorous… Giocosamente, playfully, etc.
Giocoso—humorously, (cf. jocose).
Merry; playful.
Molto,-a (It.) Much, very; as molto adagio, very slowly; molto allegro, very fast.
Molto—much, or very much. Molto cresc.—very much louder.
much, very much, a lot; very, really, very much
Italienska: #mycket
Poco (It.) A little… Poco a poco, little by little, gradually
Poco—little. Poco a poco—little by little.
little by little; gradually
Sempre (It.) Always, throughout.
Sempre—always, or continually. Sempre forte—a long passage to be played forte throughout its entirety.
always, still; maintaining the same style
Italienska: #alltid, jämt
Subitamente, Subito (It.) Suddenly, quickly
Subito—suddenly.
Suddenly, abruptly.
